The Dark Energy Survey (DES) has identified approximately 100,000 Low Surface Brightness Galaxies (LSBGs), which are characterized by their low surface brightness and low luminosity. These properties suggest that LSBGs may be dominated by dark matter, making them ideal candidates for investigating dark matter physics. This study utilizes the Y3 DES data to analyze LSBG groups, focusing on the velocity dispersion of member galaxies to constrain the dark matter density parameter ($\rho_{\rm DM}$) and dark matter density ($\sigma_{\rm DM}$). Our results indicate that LSBG groups with masses exceeding $10^{12} M_{\odot}$ exhibit velocity dispersions of roughly 100 km/s, which aligns with the predictions of the $\Lambda$CDM model. Furthermore, we find that LSBGs are more abundant in the outer regions of the groups, suggesting that the dark matter density profile follows a Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) distribution. Finally, we demonstrate that LSBGs can serve as a powerful tool for constraining dark matter density parameters, offering a complementary approach to other dark matter detection methods.

This study introduces a new method for concept positioning that utilizes crowdsourced data to generate automatic questions aimed at clarifying a concept's ambiguity. The proposed approach, QUICKAR, operates through three main stages: first, it constructs a knowledge graph to map relationships between concepts; second, it employs a graph-based model to identify highly related concepts within the knowledge structure; and finally, it leverages this selected information to generate inquiries that reduce ambiguity regarding the target concept.

This study introduces a novel preconditioner for the linear systems that emerge when applying the standard finite element method to multidimensional Darcy flow equations. Designed to withstand significant variations in key physical constants, the preconditioner enables the use of a single fixed number of preconditioning iterations across a wide range of parameters. Its effectiveness is supported by both rigorous theoretical analysis and comprehensive numerical experiments.

This study introduces a novel zero-shot abstractive discussion summarization framework. Our approach leverages discourse connection theory to restructure conversational flows into categorized groups, which are subsequently fed into a large language model for summarization. This method offers a distinct advantage by eliminating the need for models trained on specific discourse connection patterns. Consequently, it enables the generation of summaries that are both concise and rich in information, while also ensuring discussions are organized according to their thematic connections. Experimental results indicate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art models, delivering summaries that are not only informative but also highly aligned with the original content.

The Cross Section Doppler Widening (CSDW) effect, a critical component of the collective behavior in plasmas, is traditionally calculated using the complex Langevin equation. This study introduces a novel approach that leverages the Deep Neural Network (DNN) framework to forecast CSDW dynamics. By training the DNN on extensive datasets generated from the original equation, the model learns the underlying physical mechanisms governing CSDW evolution. This data-driven method significantly accelerates computation time while maintaining high accuracy. Furthermore, by integrating DNNs with the DNN-Kramers equation, we develop a Physically Informed DNN (PINN) to model the CSDW process. This hybrid approach not only enhances prediction precision but also enables the model to extrapolate to scenarios beyond its initial training data.

This paper introduces the concept of $n$-pre-Lie algebras, a generalization of pre-Lie algebras that incorporates parameters up to $n$. We present various characterizations of this new algebraic structure and define a left-symmetry product derived from $n$-Lie algebras, which serves as a generalization of Left-Symmetry products in the context of $n$-ary operations. We establish that this derived left-symmetry product is non-degenerate whenever the original $n$-Lie algebra is so, and we demonstrate that the direct sum of the underlying vector spaces forms an associative algebra that naturally carries the structure of both $n$-Lie and left-symmetry algebras.

Cell-free massive MIMO networks are increasingly recognized as a viable solution for future wireless systems, offering superior performance compared to traditional cellular architectures. However, the heterogeneous nature of cell-free deployments necessitates diverse Quality of Service (QoS) levels, a challenge that existing literature has largely overlooked. This paper introduces a joint optimization framework designed to manage these varied QoS requirements by determining optimal power allocation and user association strategies. The objective is to maximize the minimum weighted sum rate across all users while adher to specific QoS constraints. This challenging problem is reformulated into a tractable, convex equivalent through a series of transformations. The resulting model is solved using a hybrid approach combining a block coordinate descent method with a penalty-based technique. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed algorithm effectively delivers the targeted QoS for all users while achieving significant energy efficiency gains.

This study examines the convergence of a broad class of translation operators acting on a metric space $X$ under the metric topology of uniform convergence. The analysis demonstrates that convergence within this topology necessitates consistent convergence across all metrics defined on $X$. Furthermore, it is shown that the uniform convergence of these translation operators is equivalent to the uniform convergence of the corresponding Riemann sums for functions with bounded variation.

We examine the microscopic origins of composition fluctuations within a sheered mixture of colloidal particles. This system is characterized by a dynamic interplay between a "hard" component that drives structural rearrangements and a "soft" component that facilitates them. Our analysis reveals that the system's behavior is governed by two distinct length scales: a correlation length associated with elastic stresses and a memory length linked to elastic relaxation. We demonstrate that the system's dynamics are controlled by the interplay between these scales and the relative proportions of the two particle types. Specifically, we identify a regime where these lengths become comparable, in which the system's response is dictated by the ratio of soft to hard particles. In this state, the system exhibits a crossover from a non-local to a local response as the fraction of soft particles increases. We further uncover a universal scaling relationship between the correlation length and memory length, which is independent of the specific sizes of the soft and hard particles. Finally, we explore the connections between these findings and the system's macroscopic memory effects, as well as the emergence of spatially heterogeneous deformation patterns.

This paper introduces a comprehensive survey of ongoing object detection, a domain that has recently gained significant traction within the computer vision community. Although the term "ongoing object detection" lacks a standardized definition, we clarify the concept by drawing parallels with traditional object detection frameworks. We begin by outlining the specific tactics and methodologies employed in ongoing detection, followed by an examination of the unique challenges inherent to this field. Finally, we conclude with a summary of current state-of-the-art techniques and potential avenues for future research.

This study examines the initial stage of medium-induced gluon radiation, specifically the $g\to c\bar{c}$ splitting process, within the BDMPS-Z framework. We derive the $q_T$-dependent splitting function for this vertex, accounting for the influence of the medium on heavy quarks. Our results demonstrate that the medium-induced heavy-quark mass plays a pivotal role in the $q_T$-splitting function, a finding that aligns with previous research on massless particles. Furthermore, we establish that the $q_T$-splitting function is sensitive to the medium's density profile, a feature that could offer valuable insights into the mechanisms of medium-induced radiation.

This study introduces a novel framework for domain generalization in image recognition, designed to enhance model generalization across unseen domains. The proposed method leverages interpretable representations to identify domain-invariant features, thereby improving robustness. Specifically, we employ attention mechanisms to weigh feature importance and combine them with self-supervised learning to generate these representations. Additionally, we implement a self-supervised approach to extract features that are invariant to domain shifts. Experimental results on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is a network of interconnected devices that exchange data to enhance human lives. However, its current security measures are insufficient, leaving it vulnerable to various attacks. Blockchain technology offers a robust solution for securing IoT by providing a decentralized, immutable, and transparent ledger for data storage. This study proposes a blockchain-based framework to improve IoT safety and awareness, specifically focusing on agent communication within limited local domains. By utilizing a consortium blockchain, the framework enables agents to exchange safety data and alerts, fostering greater inter-agent awareness. Furthermore, the framework employs a consensus algorithm to verify and record transactions on the blockchain, ensuring the integrity of the system.

$\alpha$-attractor models are renowned for their ability to generate the observed near-scale-invariance in the CMB power spectrum while maintaining a low number of free parameters. This paper examines the slow-roll expansion within $\alpha$-attractor models, demonstrating that the leading-order predictions align with the standard approach. We establish a framework for constructing higher-order terms in this expansion and apply it to the class of $\alpha$-attractor models. We demonstrate that the resulting perturbations in the scalar and tensor sectors adhere to the standard slow-roll formalism, with parameters that are fully determined by the model's specific functions. We then apply this methodology to the specific cases of the Starobinsky, Kähler, and de Sitter models, revealing that the leading-order slow-expansion predictions for inflationary observables are consistent with the standard approach. We further explore the implications of these higher-order corrections for the inflationary potential and the generation of primordial gravitational waves.

Machine learning (ML) has become a ubiquitous tool for solving complex problems across diverse domains, including computer vision, natural language processing, and bioinformatics. While the proliferation of GPUs has significantly accelerated ML research, CPUs remain essential for various tasks, such as data preprocessing, postprocessing, and serving applications. Intel's Xeon processors, specifically those within the Scalable Family 2000, are increasingly utilized in these scenarios. This paper presents a comprehensive suite of optimization techniques for optimizing ML frameworks on Intel Xeon processors. We evaluated our methods using TensorFlow and PyTorch, focusing on both CPU-only execution and hybrid CPU-GPU environments. Our findings demonstrate that applying these optimization strategies can enhance performance by up to 1.7x on CPUs and 1.5x on hybrid configurations.

In Bayesian statistics, the Bay factor (BF) is commonly used to quantify evidence for a hypothesis, with the Bay factor for point hypotheses frequently equated to the Bay factor for a Region of Practical Equivalence (ROPE). This equivalence is often justified by the fact that the Bay factor can be expressed as the ratio of the probability of the hypothesis to the complement (i.e., BF = P(H) / P(H^c)). However, this formulation is only valid when the hypothesis is point null, as it fails to account for continuous distributions where the probability of a specific value is zero. In this study, we demonstrate that the Bay factor, the Highest Density Interval (HDI), and the ROPE are nearly identical in their mathematical relationships, allowing for precise reverse engineering among them. We illustrate this by showing how one can calculate the BF directly from the HDI and ROPE, and conversely, derive the HDI and ROPE from the BF. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the interpretation of statistical results and the potential for misinterpretation.

This study introduces a novel vector-quantized semantic communication framework. Unlike conventional methods that rely on pre-trained models, our system learns both the source message representation and the receiver's interpretation directly from the training data. The system's core components, including the quantization module, are jointly optimized to minimize the mean squared error between the input messages and the reconstructed outputs. Furthermore, we examine the impact of varying quantization bitrates on system performance and evaluate the approach using both synthetic and real-world image datasets.

Data analytics has become a cornerstone of modern society, with vast amounts of data generated daily across numerous domains. While this trend is accelerating, it is increasingly becoming a challenge due to the "Big Data" phenomenon, which is characterized by data that is large in volume, diverse in form, and difficult to process. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop new analytical methods and tools capable of handling these complexities. However, despite the significant progress made in recent years, current solutions often fall short of being user-friendly, flexible, or effective in delivering tangible results. This paper reviews the latest advancements in data analytics and identifies key challenges and opportunities for future research.
This paper introduces a categorical framework for formalizing methods within abstract theories, utilizing the comonad structure to characterize their interrelationships.

Time series analysis is a critical area of statistical research, particularly for forecasting and anomaly detection. While Time Autoregression (AR) models are standard for univariate data, Clustered Autoregression (CAR) has emerged as a leading approach for spatially correlated data. However, traditional CAR models are constrained by their fixed, low-dimensional structures, which often fail to accommodate the high-dimensional complexities of modern big data. To address this, we introduce the Visual Helper Clustered Autoregression (VH-CAR) framework, a Bayesian nonparametric extension designed to enhance the flexibility of standard CAR models. VH-CAR identifies optimal groupings of spatial units by leveraging a visual helper network, which is trained using a novel loss function that simultaneously optimizes both the grouping structure and the autoregressive parameters. Furthermore, we develop a tailored Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to efficiently sample from the posterior distribution of the visual helper network. Empirical evaluations on both simulated datasets and real-world cases demonstrate that VH-CAR outperforms existing methods in terms of predictive accuracy.

The task of verifying academic claims involves determining whether a supporting premise exists within a provided paragraph. While current methods typically rely on retrieving a proof representation from the text via a similarity-based nearest-neighbor approach, we demonstrate that this strategy is suboptimal for this specific task. We introduce a novel framework for acquiring proof representations that incorporates a scoring mechanism to rank candidate premises and a re-ranking mechanism to refine the initial retrieval results. Our proposed system achieves state-of-the-art performance on the FEVER dataset, improving the baseline nearest-neighbor approach by 10.5 percentage points.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive imaging technique capable of generating high-resolution, three-dimensional representations of the retina. While manual segmentation of retinal layers is a common approach to extract quantitative biomarkers for diagnosing retinal diseases, this process is both labor-intensive and prone to errors. To address this, we propose an automated method for segmenting the posterior segment of the eye and extracting quantitative biomarkers from OCT scans. Our approach utilizes a deep learning framework to predict segmentation masks and subsequently employs a novel algorithm to automatically extract quantitative biomarkers. Evaluated on a dataset of 1,000 OCT images, our method achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.89 for segmentation and a Mean Squared Error of 0.04 for the biomarkers.

We introduce a new neural superstatistics framework designed to model fluctuating cognitive processes. This approach integrates Bayesian inference with deep learning to estimate time-varying models of cognition from neural recordings. Theoretically, we demonstrate that this framework is equivalent to a hierarchical Bayesian model featuring a superstatistics prior, which serves as a principled method for capturing model fluctuations. Practically, we employ a neural network to approximate the posterior distribution of the models' fluctuating parameters. This strategy offers a distinct advantage over standard Bayesian inference by significantly reducing computational costs. The proposed method is validated using both simulated data and intracranial recordings from humans performing a working memory task. Results indicate that the superstatistics framework effectively uncovers fluctuating cognitive models, including a fluctuating drift rate in drift-diffusion models. Furthermore, we observe that the superstatistics prior enhances model selection accuracy compared to conventional hierarchical Bayesian inference.

This paper introduces a novel method for generating the exponents required by the Exponentiation Test (Primality Test) associated with Mersenne primes. The approach presented is straightforward, yielding an explicit formula for these exponents.

This work introduces a novel kinetic model designed to simulate the dynamics of a dilute gas interacting with a localized, time-dependent potential. The model's evolution equation is a Fokker-Planck equation featuring a non-linear collision operator, which is constructed as a perturbative expansion of the Boltzmann operator. This formulation is specifically tailored to capture the interaction mechanisms between the potential and the gas particles. We demonstrate that the solution to this kinetic model converges to a unique weak solution of the Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ in the hydrodynamic limit, where the Knudsen number approaches zero. Furthermore, we establish precise convergence rates for both the macroscopic hydrodynamic profiles and the individual particle distribution functions.

The subthermal excitation of atomic fine structure lines in the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies is a well-established phenomenon. This study examines the physical drivers behind this effect and its observational consequences, specifically focusing on the C I triplet lines at 1561, 1565, and 1733 nm. We demonstrate that the ratio of the 1733 nm line intensity to the combined 1561 and 1565 nm line intensity, denoted as $R_{C I}$, is a highly reliable and robust metric for quantifying the degree of subthermal excitation. This ratio is largely insensitive to variations in the kinetic temperature of the gas, the specific density structure, or the distribution of the molecular gas. Furthermore, the ratio $R_{C I}$ exhibits a strong correlation with the kinetic temperature, making it a valuable tool for estimating the temperature of the molecular gas. We also show that the ratio of the 1561 nm line intensity to the combined 1561, 1565, and 1733 nm line intensity, denoted as $R_{C I}^{\prime}$, serves as a reliable indicator of the gas density. Consequently, the C I triplet lines offer a powerful means to probe the physical conditions of the molecular gas reservoirs in galaxies.

Code-switching involves using two or more languages within a single utterance, a phenomenon that is increasingly common in multilingual societies. This study introduces the inaugural treebank for Verbal Frisian-Dutch code-mixing, a dialect of the Frisian language spoken in the province of Friesland, the Netherlands. The dataset comprises 1,000 sentences annotated with the Universal Dependencies framework. We outline the specific challenges of annotating code-mixed text and detail our methodology for resolving them. Additionally, we present a rule-based system designed to separate the Frisian and Dutch components of Verbal Frisian, evaluating the system's performance. Finally, we explore various natural language processing tasks utilizing this new treebank.

This study investigates the influence of stellar mass on photoevaporation within protoplanetary disks. We utilize a 1D hydrodynamic model to simulate the evolution of disks around stars ranging from 0.1 to 0.5 solar masses, assuming a power-law spectral energy distribution for the stellar radiation field. Our results indicate that the disk lifetime scales with stellar mass as $t_{\rm ev} \propto M_*$, a relationship that aligns with observational data. We further demonstrate that the mass dependence of the disk lifetime is primarily driven by the stellar mass, rather than the star's metallicity. Additionally, we calculate the mass of gas lost from the disk during photoevaporation, revealing that the evaporation mass loss rate is directly proportional to the stellar mass. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for planet formation.

This study introduces a novel, explicit high-order generalized-$\alpha$ method for structural dynamics, designed to accommodate high-order spatial discretizations. The approach is derived by integrating the generalized-$\alpha$ method with the generalized-Radial Basis Function (RBF)-Petrov-Galerkin technique, which offers an alternative framework for constructing high-order methods. The numerical results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior accuracy and enhanced stability characteristics compared to the standard Newmark method and the conventional generalized-$\alpha$ method applied to $p$-FEM.

The Bose polaron, defined as an impurity immersed in a bath of bosons, serves as a fundamental many-body system for investigating interactions within ultracold atomic gases. This study examines the decay of polaronic residues in a one-dimensional twin-well configuration, where the left well houses the polaron and the right well acts as an adjacent reservoir. We analyze the dynamics of both inter- and intra-band excitations, revealing that intra-band processes dominate the decay process. Specifically, intra-band excitations are found to be most effective when the polaron resides in a highly populated band, whereas interband excitations become significant in regimes of strong coupling. These findings are validated through a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

This study addresses the logistical challenge of distributing aid to disaster victims, a problem that is particularly difficult due to the high uncertainty surrounding the scale of destruction and the needs of the affected population. To tackle this, we developed a multi-phase, stochastic optimization framework designed to create adaptive distribution plans. The approach is divided into three phases: first, a predictive phase that estimates the extent of damage and identifies specific requirements; second, an optimization phase that generates a tailored plan based on the predicted data; and third, an adaptive phase that fine-tune the plan in real-time as new information emerges. We evaluated this framework using a simulation model built on the open-source AnyLogic platform. The results indicate that this three-phase method outperforms traditional deterministic planning approaches by effectively mitigating uncertainty and adapting to evolving information.

Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are currently detecting gravitational wave (GW) signals from a stochastic background, likely caused by a population of supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs). While the standard assumption is that these sources are circular, observational evidence suggests that real binaries may remain eccentric. This study presents a new, fully relativistic method for generating continuous gravitational waveforms for merging SMBHBs that incorporate both orbital decay and eccentricity. We validate our waveforms against existing models and assess their computational efficiency. Our findings indicate that the proposed waveforms are highly accurate for eccentricities below 0.1 and remain sufficiently precise for higher values (0.1 to 0.4) to capture post-Newtonian corrections. Additionally, we demonstrate that the computational cost of our waveforms is significantly lower than that of existing alternatives.

This paper introduces a novel method for analyzing activities within global programming contests. It leverages a unique dataset comprising 1.2 million submissions from 35,000 developers across 20 years of competition history. The proposed approach utilizes an activity metric derived from submission timing and coding complexity to identify participants' actions. This method examines the behavioral patterns of both individual developers and teams, revealing that a significant portion of submissions are dedicated to non-competitive tasks. Furthermore, the study investigates how developer actions influence contest outcomes and uncovers specific behavioral trends among top-tier competitors.

This study introduces a new method for analyzing high-viscosity liquids within millimeter-wave integrated circuits (ICs) using coplanar transmission lines. The technique leverages the frequency-dependent attenuation of the signal traveling through the liquid. The method's efficacy is demonstrated by measuring the attenuation of a 750–1100 GHz signal in glycerol, a substance known for its high attenuation. The results show that the measured attenuation aligns with theoretical predictions based on the liquid's viscosity, confirming the method's accuracy.

The global COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant devastation, prompting the development of various strategies to mitigate its impact. This paper introduces a framework designed to evaluate the efficacy of these approaches by leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms and multi-source data analysis. The proposed system integrates diverse data streams—including weather conditions, mobility patterns, and social media activity—to forecast infection rates and guide policy decisions. By applying AI techniques, such as machine learning and natural language processing, the framework aims to identify emerging trends and potential outbreaks. Ultimately, this approach offers a comprehensive and adaptable solution for policymakers seeking to enhance their pandemic response strategies.

This study introduces a novel, multi-scale Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) framework designed to simulate multi-phase fluid-structure interactions. The approach employs a hybrid particle method that integrates a standard SPH scheme for the bulk fluid regions with a high-order Moving Least Squares (HOL-MLS) technique near solid boundaries. This combination ensures the satisfaction of the kinematic and dynamic no-slip boundary conditions. The proposed method was tested against various benchmark scenarios, including the interaction between two immiscible fluids and a flexible structure, as well as the impact of a water jet on a flexible structure. The results demonstrate that the hybrid approach offers superior accuracy compared to conventional methods, particularly in resolving the sharp velocity gradients that occur at the interface between a fluid and a solid.

Nodal surfaces (NSs) represent closed three-dimensional (3D) regions within a material's momentum space where a specific energy band vanishes. These structures are topologically protected against perturbations that maintain time-reversal symmetry, making them a subject of intense interest in condensed matter physics. This review examines the topological attributes of NSs, highlighting their recent experimental realization in photonic systems. Particular focus is placed on the topological invariants governing NSs and their associated monopole characteristics. Additionally, the article explores the unique physical phenomena enabled by these structures, including the formation of nontrivial light cones, the generation of topological edge states, and the creation of nonreciprocal effects.
This report presents the findings of the HL-LHC computing evaluation, specifically addressing the stage-2 software initiatives related to event generators.

This work establishes both necessary and sufficient criteria for an infinite abelian group $G$ to possess invariant characteristics associated with average operators defined on finite subsets. Specifically, it is demonstrated that $G$ exhibits these properties—meaning there exists a non-zero bounded function $f:2^{(G)}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that the partial average operator $\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{a\in A}f(a+a')$ remains invariant under the translation action of every element $a\in G$—if and only if $G$ is either finite or isomorphic to a direct sum of a divisible group and a direct limit of discrete countable groups.

This study presents the first observational confirmation of a dense disk of dark molecular matter in the outer regions of the Milky Way. By analyzing the 12CO J=1-0 emission line from the outer Galaxy, we identified a substantial dark molecular disk with a mass of approximately $1.5 \times 10^8$ solar masses, extending to a radius of about 15 kpc. This disk is characterized by a high mass-to-light ratio of roughly 100, significantly exceeding that of the stellar population. The spatial distribution of this dark disk is notably more extended than that of the stellar disk, which is consistent with the observed distribution of the dark matter halo. Furthermore, the dark molecular disk is more massive than the visible molecular gas disk, which has a mass of only about $1.5 \times 10^7$ solar masses. The existence of such a massive dark molecular disk in the outer Galaxy suggests that dark molecular matter may be a significant component of the dark matter halo, challenging the traditional view that dark matter is purely baryonic.

This study examines the correlation between compensation and service levels within a restricted economic framework. The model incorporates an entity offering a fixed service level and a competitive rival offering one that is both higher and variable. Assuming the market's size is determined solely by its price- and service-elasticities, we derive the competitor's optimal strategy and establish the conditions under which the fixed service level proves most beneficial.

This study investigates the collective behavior of disordered polar active matter, utilizing a framework that integrates both interactions and steric hindrance. We demonstrate that the combination of steric forces and polar alignment generates a unique phase characterized by a disordered yet dense state, which we term the "thick disordered phase." This phase is distinct from the standard isotropic fluid because it exhibits significantly reduced mobility and displays anomalous diffusion. Furthermore, we observe that the transition from normal to anomalous diffusion is not a direct shift but occurs via an intermediate disordered solid state.

Semileptonic transitions involving doubly charmed baryons are investigated using the Pochat model. Within this framework, the hadronic matrix elements are determined by expressing the doubly charmed baryon wave functions as linear combinations of single charmed baryon wave functions. The study focuses on semileptonic decays of the $\Xi_{cc}^{\pm}$, $\Omega_{cc}^{\pm}$, and $\Xi_{cc}^{0}$ baryons into single charmed baryons, specifically the $N_c$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$, $N_c^*$,

This study introduces a new paradigm for positioning, wherein an autonomous agent determines its location through dialogue with a human partner. The human provides spatial descriptions of landmarks relative to the agent, which the agent must interpret to identify its own position. We conducted a study with 20 participants to evaluate this approach, assessing both the frequency of successful positioning and the accuracy of the derived coordinates. Results indicate that leveraging dialogic interaction yields a positioning success rate of 85%, with the majority of failures stemming from insufficient conversation length. Furthermore, analysis of the generated dialogues revealed that agents employ a specific vocabulary of spatial terms and movement actions, which significantly correlates with positioning accuracy. These findings offer initial evidence supporting the viability of embodiment-based conversation for positioning tasks.

Vibration analysis is a widely used technique for monitoring rotating machinery, yet selecting the appropriate frequency band for evaluation remains a critical challenge. While various methodologies exist, they often rely on subjective decisions or established standards, which may not always be optimal for specific scenarios. This paper introduces a novel automatic approach to frequency band selection based on vibration assessment. The method utilizes a proposed Band Significance Factor (BSF), which aggregates frequency band-specific metrics such as Kurtosis, Peak Factor (PF), Crest Factor (CF), and the Peak-to-RMS Ratio (PR). The authors validate the BSF's effectiveness through a case study on a motor's bearing fault diagnosis. The results demonstrate that the BSF successfully isolates the relevant frequency band, thereby enhancing the precision of fault identification.

This study employs muon-spin relaxation (μSR) to investigate the superconducting states of the noncentrosymmetric compounds CaIrSi₃ and CaPtSi₃. The μSR findings reveal that both materials exhibit a zero-field superconducting base state, which is consistent with the absence of spontaneous magnetic fields. Furthermore, the temperature dependence of the superfluid density, normalized to its value at absolute zero, aligns well with BCS predictions for both compounds. However, the superconducting transition temperatures ($T_c$) observed in μSR for these materials are significantly lower than those reported in other studies. This discrepancy is attributed to the muon probe's sensitivity to the local superfluid density, which is influenced by disorder-induced fluctuations in the order parameter.

The Sparse Grid Attributes Method (SGAM) is a novel, data-driven approach designed to mitigate the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional optimal control problems. This work introduces a new algorithm that integrates the standard Sparse Grid Attributes Method with the Dynamic Programming Principle (DPP) to solve the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation for stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) control. The resulting SGAM-DP algorithm is capable of handling systems with numerous states and controls, as well as those involving non-Gaussian noise. Furthermore, the method is extended to address mean-field LQ control, specifically for determining optimal responses in systems with numerous followers. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed SGAM-DP algorithm outperforms existing methods in both accuracy and efficiency.

We introduce a novel framework for classifying quantum states, which leverages higher-dimensional quantum systems known as qudits. This method utilizes qudits to encode the count of specific states belonging to a particular class. We demonstrate that this approach can effectively execute logical operations, such as addition and multiplication, by employing qudits within a larger quantum network. Furthermore, this proposed scheme is capable of performing both classical and quantum computations.

This study introduces a unified framework for modeling and managing multi-energy dynamic systems, with a specific focus on the interconnected dynamics of electricity, natural gas, and heating networks. The primary objective is to determine the optimal operational strategies for these systems, thereby facilitating the transition toward decarbonization. To achieve this, we develop a comprehensive model that integrates the physical characteristics of each network component, including their temporal dependencies, interconnections, and inherent uncertainties. This modeling approach is applied to a specific case study involving an integrated multi-energy system. Furthermore, we formulate a hierarchical optimization strategy designed to address the operational challenges posed by such systems. This strategy is evaluated using a representative case study, demonstrating its effectiveness in managing complex, coupled energy infrastructures.

This study examines the application of machine learning to the two-dimensional filtration model, a nonlinear integro-differential equation governing the evolution of a fluid-saturated porous medium's permeability. The analysis focuses on scenarios where the initial permeability profile is unknown, proposing a strategy to infer this function from observational data. The paper outlines a computational framework that combines a numerical solver for the equation with a regression-based approach to approximate the initial conditions.

This study introduces a rapid magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technique for visualizing heat distribution within a gas-solid packed bed reactor. The method employs a compact, low-cost system capable of generating high temporal resolution images of the gas temperature, which is measured non-invasively by tracking the gas's magnetic susceptibility. The system's performance was validated using a simple test bench, a transparent column containing glass beads and heated by a single heat source. The MRI setup was then applied to a real industrial catalytic reactor, a device used for partial oxidation of ethylene to ethylene oxide. The results demonstrate that this approach can effectively monitor heat transfer dynamics in both experimental and operational settings, offering a valuable tool for analyzing and optimizing such processes.

We introduce a theoretical framework for reentrant superconductivity in the context of fluctuating order parameters, specifically examining the heavy fermion candidate UTe$_2$. Our analysis indicates that the superconducting phase diagram exhibits a reentrant region at elevated temperatures, a prediction that aligns with experimental findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a reentrant transition can arise from the interplay of disorder and thermal fluctuations, even in the absence of a first-order scenario.

Ultra-wideband (UWB) technology is a radio frequency standard designed for transmitting data across a wide spectrum. While it offers significant advantages, such as high data rates and immunity to interference, its performance is heavily dependent on the specific PHY configuration. To fully leverage these benefits, the PHY configuration must be optimized for the current radio environment. This paper introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach to automatically adjust PHY parameters in real-time. The method utilizes the A3C algorithm to select the optimal configuration for a given environment, with experimental results demonstrating that the A3C agent achieves performance comparable to a human expert.

This study examines the k-median grouping problem within discrete Fréchet and Hausdorff metrics, where the objective is to assign a set of input points to $k$ groups such that the sum of the group representatives' distances (medians) to their assigned points is minimized. The paper establishes that this problem is NP-hard for both metrics, even when the points are restricted to a line, and proves the problem remains NP-hard under a Hausdorff metric with just two groups. Furthermore, the authors present a polynomial-time algorithm for the k-median problem under discrete Fréchet distance that runs in $O^*(2^k)$ time, and extend this approach to achieve an $O^*(k^k)$ complexity for k-partitioning under the Hausdorff metric.

This paper introduces a novel framework for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) that leverages primal-dual optimization to resolve a specific game-theoretic formulation of the MARL problem. This approach is designed to overcome the limitations of traditional value iteration, which is often inapplicable due to the absence of known transition probabilities in the state space. By employing a single-player game where the state is the average of the agents' policies, the method aims to discover a Nash equilibrium that corresponds to a joint policy maximizing the expected average reward. The framework utilizes double-averaging techniques to ensure the convergence of the primal-dual algorithm. Theoretical analysis confirms that the method achieves an optimal convergence rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the average reward, with $T$ representing the total number of iterations. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the algorithm also converges to a Nash equilibrium with a convergence rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the average policy distance. Empirical evaluations across various MARL tasks validate the method's effectiveness and superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper introduces a coalgebraic framework for the validity verification of $\mu$-calculi, extending the work in [1]. We define a class of arithmetic $\mu$-calculi, $\mathcal{L}$, which are interpreted within the context of $\Sigma$-algebras. We demonstrate that the set of $\mathcal{L}$-valid sentences is recursively enumerable whenever $\Sigma$ is an effectively many-one algebra. This result is achieved by constructing a transition system that is both sound and complete for the $\mathcal{L}$-validity problem, alongside establishing a sufficient condition for this system's decidability. We illustrate the applicability of our framework by examining two specific cases: the validity problem for first-order arithmetic logic and that for the fragment of arithmetic logic restricted to bounded quantifiers.

This study introduces a new approach for estimating sparse initial conditions in partial differential equations (PDEs) by leveraging low-rank tensor methods. The technique is designed to handle PDEs defined over high-dimensional domains, such as those arising in isogeometric analysis (IGA). In IGA, basis functions are constructed via a tensor product of univariate polynomials, which naturally induces a low-rank structure on the resulting initial condition. We demonstrate that this property allows the initial state to be represented efficiently as a compact low-rank tensor. The proposed reconstruction algorithm operates in two phases: first, it utilizes the observed data points to build a data matrix, and second, it applies a truncated SVD to this matrix to recover the initial condition. Theoretically, we establish that the low-rank approximation derived from the truncated SVD converges to the true initial state as the amount of data increases. Furthermore, numerical experiments are presented to validate the method's effectiveness and to confirm its ability to accurately reconstruct initial conditions for PDEs in high-dimensional spaces governed by IGA.

This study introduces a drive-through air quality monitoring system designed to efficiently map the spatial distribution of pollutants across a city. The core challenge involves selecting an optimal subset of vehicles to traverse specific routes, thereby enabling the estimation of air quality at all monitoring sites. The selection mechanism is formulated as a facility location problem, where each potential route is modeled as a demand point and each vehicle as a facility. The objective is to minimize the weighted sum of distances between assigned vehicles and unmonitored sites. The resulting air quality chart is compact, representing the city's conditions with a minimal set of data points. The system's efficiency is demonstrated through a case study of a city in the United States.

The domain consists of characteristics $p$ where $p$ is an odd prime dividing the class number $2k+1$ with $p \geq 3$, utilizing ring truncations of degree at least $2k+1$. The Weil vector space is defined as the space of functions on the ring that are invariant under the action of the symplectic group. The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has sparked widespread adoption across numerous sectors, including education, healthcare, and entertainment. In entertainment, AI-driven video generation has become increasingly popular, offering a cost-effective and efficient solution for producing high-quality visual content. This technology empowers creators to generate high-fidelity videos with minimal manual intervention, thereby streamlining workflows and enhancing productivity. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the latest AI-driven video generation methods, encompassing text-to-video, image-to-video, and video editing techniques. We critically examine the underlying architectures, datasets, and evaluation metrics associated with these approaches. Furthermore, we outline the practical applications of these tools and identify key challenges that remain unsolved. Finally, we propose potential future research directions to address current limitations.

This study examines the squeezed coherent states of ions within quadrupole and octopole traps. We derive the Hamiltonian for a single ion under these fields and employ the Gell-Mann and Myers method to generate the corresponding squeezed coherent states. Additionally, we calculate the average energy, the variance of the radial component, and the radial distribution function for these states. Our findings indicate that the radial distribution function can be modulated by adjusting the squeezing parameter, thereby enabling the ion's spatial probability distribution to be tailored according to specific experimental requirements.

Neuroscience-inspired frameworks have been developed to address challenges in machine learning, specifically the need for models that are both interpretable and capable of learning efficiently with limited data. However, the performance of these frameworks is highly sensitive to their specific hyper-parameters, which can be difficult to identify without prior knowledge. Consequently, this study examines the impact of hyper-parameter selection on the performance of various neuroscience models by utilizing a Bayesian optimization approach known as "Learning to Learn." The research evaluates how this method can assist in selecting optimal hyper-parameters for neuroscience models, with a specific focus on the Deep Hierarchical Temporal Memory (DH-STM) system. The results demonstrate that Learning to Learn is effective in identifying high-performing hyper-parameters for DH-STM, thereby reducing the time and effort required for manual parameter tuning.

Camouflaged object segmentation (COS) is a demanding computer vision challenge that has garnered significant attention in recent years. However, existing COS datasets are limited in scale and suffer from poor annotation quality, which hinders the development of robust techniques and the evaluation of real-world performance. To address these limitations, we introduce COSD, a comprehensive Camouflaged Object Segmentation dataset comprising 1,000 images with high-quality annotations. This collection features diverse categories, including animals, plants, insects, and man-made objects, and is designed to simulate real-world scenarios. To facilitate research, we also provide a benchmark toolkit that supports various evaluation metrics, such as the newly proposed "objectness" score. Extensive experiments using this toolkit reveal that current state-of-the-art methods struggle to effectively segment camouflaged objects. To encourage further innovation, we have released the dataset and tools publicly at https://github.com/ChenyuChen1997/COSD.

This study examines the effects of Lorentz violation on the superconducting state, specifically analyzing how such a violation alters the energy gap and the critical temperature. The violation is incorporated into the BCS framework by modifying the two-particle scattering amplitude. Our findings indicate that the energy gap is reduced by this Lorentz violation, and consequently, the critical temperature also decreases due to this reduction in the energy gap.

AI systems are increasingly integrated into critical decision-making processes, yet their inherent opacity and susceptibility to errors make identifying mistakes challenging. This study introduces a novel methodology for detecting AI faults by leveraging crowdsourced reporting. We evaluated this approach using a crowdsourced dataset of defect reports for Amazon Rekognition, a widely used image recognition service. Our analysis reveals that human annotators successfully identified 1,000 genuine defects within 1,000 trials, achieving a high level of precision. To validate these findings, we verified 1,000 of these reported issues by cross-referencing them with Amazon Rekognition's error logs, ultimately confirming 1,000 of these reports. This paper presents a novel approach to uncovering AI faults through human-in-the-loop testing, demonstrating that a large-scale, distributed effort can effectively identify and verify significant numbers of these errors. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become the standard for object recognition, yet their inherent sequential processing limits performance. To address this, researchers have developed parallel CNNs, which concurrently execute multiple layers to enhance efficiency. However, this approach often results in excessive computational waste, as every layer must process all input data regardless of its relevance. To mitigate this inefficiency, we introduce Stochastic Choice Routing for Object Recognition (R(Det)^2), a novel framework that dynamically routes data to relevant layers based on a probabilistic model. This model is trained to predict the likelihood of each object's presence, enabling CNNs to focus computational resources on pertinent parts of the image. We evaluated R(Det)^2 against leading state-of-the-art CNNs on the PASCAL VOC 2012 dataset. Results demonstrate that our framework achieves a 10% reduction in computational cost while maintaining comparable accuracy to top-tier models.

Adversarial training is a standard method for enhancing the robustness of deep neural networks, yet it often results in significant accuracy drops. This study examines Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) attacks and reveals that catastrophic overfitting occurs when adversarial examples are generated from a single batch. This issue stems from the fact that the gradient norm of a single, unregularized sample can be excessively large, causing the model to overfit to noise within that specific example. To address this, we introduce ZeroGrad, a straightforward yet effective technique that zeroes out the gradient of a single sample whenever its norm surpasses a certain threshold. Experiments demonstrate that ZeroGrad mitigates catastrophic overfitting, yielding an improvement of 1.5% to 2.5% in clean accuracy on ImageNet compared to standard FGSM training. Furthermore, we show that ZeroGrad can be applied to any gradient-based attack, and ablation studies indicate that this approach also helps mitigate the phenomenon of "catastrophic forgetting" in adversarially trained models.

This study examines the Thakurta metric, a black hole solution within $f(R)$ gravity, to evaluate its physical viability. We demonstrate that the metric fails to describe a black hole because it lacks a black hole horizon, and we further argue that recent claims limiting primordial black hole (PBH) abundance based on gravitational wave detections from the LIGO-Virgo collaboration are invalid. Ultimately, the constraints on PBHs derived from these observations remain unaffected by this analysis.

This study examines how persistent asset changes affect Swarm Intelligence (SI) optimization methods inspired by hybrid systems. We specifically analyze the impact on the Hybrid Whale Optimization Algorithm (HWOA) and Hybrid Particle Swarm Optimization (HPSO) by introducing a novel mechanism that retains the best-found solution across multiple independent runs. This approach aims to mitigate the detrimental effects of volatile, non-persistent environmental fluctuations. We evaluate these algorithms on a comprehensive suite of 10 benchmark test functions, each featuring a distinct form of transient noise. The results demonstrate that the incorporation of an asset retention mechanism significantly enhances the performance of both HWOA and HPSO.

Bootstrapping represents a pivotal challenge in developing practical Completely Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) systems. This paper introduces a novel method for the bootstrapping phase of FHE, designed to function efficiently on contemporary hardware. The approach utilizes a "propeller" structure, where the keyswitching operation is reconfigured to align with the specific structure of ciphertext noise distributions. This strategy significantly reduces the computational overhead associated with the process. Additionally, the method demonstrates robustness across various plaintext moduli sizes. Experimental results indicate that our technique achieves a 1.5x to 2.5x performance improvement over current state-of-the-art bootstrapping methods.

This work examines the partition function of a random matrix ensemble featuring a general potential, subject to the constraint that all diagonal elements are non-negative. The analysis reveals that the resulting partition function is a rational expression, with the denominator being a matrix integral defined over the dimension of the system. We derive the partition function for this denominator in cases where the unconstrained potential is linear, identifying it as a combination of Bessel functions. Furthermore, we calculate the distributions of the resulting eigenvalues for two specific scenarios: the standard Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble and the Bessel orthogonal ensemble.

This study introduces a method for experimentally investigating quantum correlations within a two-qutrit system, utilizing a scheme based on the $^{171}\text{Yb}^{+}$ ion. The protocol relies on the specific energy level structure of the ion to generate two distinct entangled states. We define a correlation function that captures the quantum connections between the qubits and employ it to analyze the correlations in both entangled configurations. The results demonstrate that the proposed correlation function effectively measures quantum connections, thereby offering a viable approach for the experimental verification of such phenomena in systems involving three-level atoms.

We present a novel theorem establishing that a bipartite quantum state is separable if and only if its measurement statistics can be accounted for by a model satisfying both locality and decomposability. Decomposability entails that a measurement operator acts on the system in such a way that it does not alter the state of the system being measured. This finding is distinct from Bell's theorem because it does not rely on any hidden variable assumptions.

StyleGAN2 has become a standard for high-quality image synthesis, yet it lacks the capability to generate videos. This paper introduces StyleGAN-V, a novel architecture capable of generating unlimited-length videos with high fidelity. Our approach extends StyleGAN2 by integrating a recurrent mechanism that leverages temporal information to refine the generator's performance. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness through extensive ablation studies and empirical tests, confirming that StyleGAN-V produces superior video quality compared to existing methods. Additionally, we release a pre-trained StyleGAN-V model along with a web-based interface for generating videos.

Accurate estimation of the exposure date is crucial for validating the reliability of dosimetry services. In the context of thermolumoluminescence (TLD) dosimetry, this involves analyzing glow curves to determine when a material was exposed to radiation. Historically, this has relied on the "shining in the dark" method, which involves adding a specific temperature step to a glow curve to check if it "shines." While effective, this approach is laborious and prone to human error. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to automate the detection of the "shining" effect. By training a convolutional neural network (CNN) on a dataset of 1,000 glow curves spanning exposure dates from 2010 to 2020, the model achieved a mean absolute error of just 1.1 years. This represents a significant improvement over the traditional method, which yielded an error of 2.5 years. Furthermore, the trained model can identify the 2016 exposure date with a probability exceeding 99%, demonstrating its potential to serve as a robust, automated tool for exposure dating in TLD operations.

We introduce a novel model interpretation method, S-LIME, designed to explain predictions from black-box classifiers. This approach is a refinement of the original LIME algorithm, which generates local linear approximations of a classifier's output around a specific instance to produce human-readable explanations. While S-LIME retains this core functionality, it introduces a stabilization mechanism that ensures the consistency of explanations across multiple runs. The proposed method is computationally efficient, requiring no additional hyperparameters, and has been validated through experiments on various datasets.

This study introduces a categorization model designed to enhance performance on categorization tasks. By employing a hierarchical Bayesian framework, the model incorporates justification feedback to refine category representations and improve the accuracy of classification decisions. It was evaluated using three datasets from the categorization task literature. The findings indicate that the model effectively replicates human performance and exhibits notable robustness against noise.

The discovery of spin liquids has driven extensive research into quantum materials, with the hexagonal compound TbInO$_3$ emerging as a leading candidate due to its geometrically frustrated triangular lattice. This material exhibits a distinctive magnetic structure characterized by a large number of degenerate ground states, yet definitive proof of a spin liquid state remains absent. This study employs inelastic neutron scattering to map out the entire magnetic excitation spectrum of TbInO$_3$. The results reveal that the low-energy spectrum is highly fragmented, indicating a crystal field-split spectrum. Furthermore, the observed excitation patterns are attributed to the coupling between magnetic excitations and vibrational modes. These findings underscore the critical role of crystal field effects and vibronic interactions in TbInO$_3$, offering new insights into the search for spin liquids.

This paper examines the evolution of mean power, $H^k$, where $k>0$, on a moving hypersurface. We demonstrate that for $k \geq 1$, the evolution of this quantity can be formulated as a heat-type equation within a convex framework. Leveraging this structure, we establish short-time existence of solutions and prove that when $k \geq 2$, the supremum of $H^k$ can blow up only at isolated points. Furthermore, we show that for $k=1$, the evolution corresponds to a heat-type equation within a non-convective framework. Finally, the paper includes an analysis of the behavior of the mean power of curvature under the mean curvature flow.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in numerous computer vision tasks, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely obscure. This paper introduces a novel framework for learning CNNs within the spectral domain. By demonstrating that convolutional layers can be equivalently represented as linear filters in the Fourier domain, we reformulate the entire CNN learning process as a sequence of linear filters learning tasks. We propose a specific algorithm to learn these linear filters and apply it to reconstruct the full CNN. Experimental results indicate that our approach achieves performance comparable to conventional CNN learning methods.

This paper introduces a new unsupervised image grouping framework designed to overcome the limitations of existing methods. While current approaches typically rely on clustering based on feature vectors derived from a single layer of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), we demonstrate that this strategy is insufficient for grouping images with diverse characteristics. To address this, we propose a multi-layer architecture that enables clustering based on features extracted from multiple CNN layers. Our approach utilizes a deep neural network to iteratively refine the grouping process across successive layers, thereby enhancing overall clustering performance. Furthermore, we incorporate a specific loss function to optimize the network parameters. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper outlines a system designed to identify organizational risks within corporate environments by leveraging an automated analysis of news data. The architecture employs knowledge graphs to structure the relationships among entities mentioned in the processed information. The study details the methodology for constructing this knowledge graph, specifically addressing the creation of a unified ontology that integrates entities from various open-source knowledge networks with the automated extraction of opinion scores from news articles. Additionally, the paper examines the system's performance, illustrated through a case study of a specific corporate network, and discusses the tool's practical applications.

This study introduces a novel approach to categorization that utilizes a new metric for quantifying the similarity between data points. This measure is constructed by analyzing the homology groups of simplicial complexes built from pairwise distances. The proposed method is validated through two real-world datasets, including one used to evaluate the performance of the proposed measure against various existing similarity metrics.

Contra similarity is defined as a symmetric and transitive equivalence relation. In this paper, we introduce the formal game-theoretic semantics for this concept and provide examples to illustrate its application.

We provide several representations of the string 2-group, which is defined as the 2-group of 2-connected E8-manifolds. Our approach involves constructing it as the semidirect product of the string group with the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ group. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the string group can be characterized as the loop group of the special orthogonal group, $SO(3)$.

This study examines the generation of rogue waves within ion-acoustic waves (IAWs) in a double pair plasma comprising non-extensive electrons and ions alongside cold, massless ions. The analysis employs the reductive perturbation method to derive the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) and its corresponding soliton and rogue wave solutions. The results indicate that IAWs are unstable in this environment, leading to the emergence of envelope solitons and ion-acoustic rogue waves. Furthermore, the impact of the non-extensive parameter on rogue wave formation is investigated, revealing that this parameter significantly influences both the amplitude and the conditions required for the formation of these waves.

The parametric decay instability (PDI) of Alfvén waves is a critical mechanism for heating and heating plasma in fusion devices, yet its behavior in laboratory settings remains poorly understood. This study investigates the PDI within a magnetized plasma environment by combining a 2D kinetic model with a 3D magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) framework. Our results indicate that the instability can be triggered by Alfvén waves with amplitudes as low as 10⁻³, and that the resulting daughter waves are significantly more intense than the parent wave. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the PDI is highly sensitive to the initial plasma temperature, with the instability being suppressed in hot plasmas. These findings offer essential insights into the role of PDI in fusion plasma heating and provide a foundation for future experimental investigations.

This study examines the gravitational instability of thread-like molecular nebulae, accounting for ambipolar diffusion. We derive a dispersion relation for a cylindrical fluid in a self-gravitating state, incorporating ambipolar diffusion effects. Our analysis reveals that this factor induces a transition in the cylinder's dynamical behavior from that of a standard fluid to a partially conducting plasma. Furthermore, we calculate the critical mass and radius thresholds required to trigger gravitational instability.

We investigate the quantum Zeno and anti-Zeno effects within the framework of a two-level system strongly coupled to a bosonic bath. Our findings indicate that, contrary to established literature, these effects are governed by the system's initial state. Specifically, frequent measurements on a system initially prepared in a state of maximum entropy result in the emergence of the anti-Zeno effect, whereas the same preparation does not yield this phenomenon under unitary evolution. Conversely, systems initialized in a pure state display a Zeno effect under both measurement strategies. Furthermore, we observe that measurement protocols can induce a transition from the anti-Zeno to the Zeno regime as the measurement interval decreases.

This study examines the thermal behavior of the one-dimensional Heisenberg model subject to both anisotropic DM interactions and an uneven external field. By applying the Bethe ansatz method, we derive the exact ground state energy and analyze the corresponding phase diagram. Our results indicate that the phase boundaries are influenced by DM interactions and field parameters, potentially yielding up to four distinct phases. Additionally, we investigate the temperature-dependent behavior of the magnetization order parameter and the spin-spin correlation function. Our findings demonstrate that the system undergoes a second-order phase transition at a critical temperature, $T_c$, which is modulated by variations in the field parameters and DM interactions.

This study introduces a distributed path planning algorithm for coordinating quadrotor swarms, ensuring collision avoidance and viability. The approach utilizes a graph-based model of the environment, where nodes represent potential flight positions and edges denote possible trajectories. To guarantee safety, we employ a linear safe passage (LSP) framework, which constrains the velocity vector within a polyhedral region to prevent both inter-vehicle collisions and ground impacts. The planning mechanism utilizes a graph search algorithm to identify a feasible trajectory for each node, with connectivity between nodes defined by the polyhedral velocity constraints imposed by the LSP framework.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has become a key area of research for addressing the significant domain gap between simulated and real-world environments, a challenge that is particularly acute in autonomous driving. While existing UDA methods have demonstrated success in transferring pre-trained models from simulators to actual roads, they often fail to generalize across diverse real-world domains. To address this, we introduce CARLANE (CarLanes Evaluation), a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the robustness of these algorithms against various target domains. CARLANE features a dataset of 1,000 images from the KITTI Road Detector, each annotated with precise road lane information. This benchmark enables the testing of UDA methods across multiple distinct domains, including wet roads, night driving, and different weather conditions. We have also developed a novel UDA framework, which we term "CARLANE," specifically designed to leverage lane data for enhancing transferability. Extensive experiments across all domains reveal that our proposed method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches, achieving a 10% to 20% improvement in performance.

Hydrogels are extensively utilized in soft robotics, yet their surface roughness often leads to a complex, diminishing contact angle that complicates wetting behavior. This study investigates how embedded particles within hydrogels can mitigate such angular variations. We developed a theoretical framework to predict the surface profile of hydrogels swollen in a solvent containing a dispersed particle phase. Our findings indicate that particle inclusion can normalize the surface, thereby stabilizing the contact angle. These results offer valuable insights for the design of soft robotic systems employing hydrogels.

The transition to remote learning caused by the pandemic has sparked significant debate regarding the impact of online education on student engagement and academic performance. This study examines the correlation between engagement and achievement within an online course, utilizing data from a 2020 online physics class taught at the University of Colorado Boulder. Engagement metrics were derived from students' participation in discussion boards, the frequency of logins, and the completion of practice quizzes. Academic performance was measured by final exam scores and final grades. Results indicate a strong positive correlation between engagement and achievement, with correlation coefficients ranging from 0.60 to 0.80. Notably, the correlation between discussion board participation and final grades was the highest, reaching 0.80. Furthermore, the analysis suggests that students who were initially higher performers in the course tended to be more engaged throughout the semester.

This study introduces an autoregressive approach to analyzing wind speed data collected by the University of Hawaii's L-band Doppler radar. The technique is designed to identify the characteristic timescales of wind speed fluctuations, which serve as a proxy for wind variability. The authors demonstrate that wind speeds across the island exhibit a consistent temporal pattern, with a peak in spectral density occurring at a period of 10 minutes. Furthermore, this method is applied to evaluate the reliability of wind speed sensors, such as anemometers, in capturing wind dynamics.

Our analysis reveals that UBC 274 is a young, kinematically distinct group with a mean radial velocity of 100 km/s, a velocity dispersion of 10 km/s, and a total mass of 1.2 x 10^4 solar masses.
